extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in prank calls, comedy, telephony, and legal aspects
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of prank phone calls covering definition, history, methods/platforms, anonymity/traceability, legal issues, harms, and cultural examples. Useful for understanding how prank calls are carried out and when they become problematic or illegal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a prank call
rubrics_metrics.description: A prank call (also known as a crank call, a hoax call, or a goof call) is a telephone call intended by the caller as a practical joke played on the person answering; it is often a type of nuisance call and can be illegal under certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets the basic evaluative boundary: intent to prank distinguishes prank calls from other phone interactions; whether it's a nuisance or rises to illegality depends on context and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity / caller identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Prank callers can be identified through caller ID, but many telephone companies permit callers to withhold identifying information using vertical service codes (e.g., *67 in North America, 141 in the UK); other techniques include payphones and VoIP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes limitations and trade-offs: victims may avoid answering ID-blocked numbers; payphones are declining; VoIP calls may be hard to trace because they pass through multiple servers, but advancing digital switching (SS7), unspoofable ANI, carrier exchange logging, and government wiretapping can make tracing easier. Use of anonymity techniques can affect detectability and legal exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods and platforms for carrying out prank calls
rubrics_metrics.description: Prank calls can be live or pre-recorded and are delivered via traditional phones, payphones, VoIP, internet radio streams, or gaming/voice-chat software; communities share calls via rotation broadcasts on SHOUTcast, Prankcast-style services, soundboards, and social platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes production/distribution choices: live vs pre-recorded affects interaction dynamics; platforms (e.g., SHOUTcast, Ventrilo, Prankcast.com, soundboards) enable broader sharing or private live prank communities; choice of platform affects reach and legal/ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal criteria for criminality
rubrics_metrics.description: Some prank calls are criminalized in many jurisdictions — for example, calls involving emergency services or those meeting statutory tests for harassment or threats; in the U.S., under 47 U.S.C. § 223(a)(1) a call must be made with intent to 'abuse, threaten, or harass' to violate that provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating legality, consider jurisdictional statutes and required mens rea (intent). Examples: false bomb threats, calls to emergency services, or calls intended to harass/abuse can be prosecutable; statutes and enforcement differ by country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcasting recorded calls and consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicly broadcasting or publishing recorded prank calls can raise legal issues — e.g., Australian authorities alleged that the 2Day FM incident violated law on the grounds the recorded call was publicly broadcast without the other party's consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers/distributors should verify consent and applicable recording/broadcast laws before publishing; broadcasting without consent may create liability even if the original call itself is lawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impersonation and posing as authority figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Posing as authority figures (police, physicians, corporate managers, fire alarm company reps) has been used in elaborate pranks (e.g., strip search phone call scam, Pranknet) and can induce victims into harmful or illegal acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impersonation greatly increases legal and ethical risk — it can lead to convictions (examples include imprisonment for impersonating a physician) and severe harm to victims; avoid impersonating officials or professionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential harms and ethical consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Prank calls have caused property damage, humiliation, financial loss, physical danger, and even suicide (e.g., the Jacintha Saldanha case); they can include threats of violence, racial epithets, or instructions that cause bodily harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate pranks not only on comedic merit but also on foreseeable harm. High-risk content (bomb threats, instructions that lead to self-harm or property damage, targeted harassment) is ethically and legally problematic and can have severe consequences for victims and callers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting tactics and social-engineering
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactics include posting phone numbers on sites like Craigslist to generate inbound calls (sometimes exploiting time zone differences), social engineering to trick recipients into actions, and using soundboards or scripts to elicit predictable responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tactics increase effectiveness but also risk: posting others' numbers can cause harassment and legal complications (platforms may not reveal posters without court orders), and social-engineering that provokes harmful behavior can be criminal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classic gag formats and comedic tropes
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-known gag structures include the 'refrigerator' gag ('Is your refrigerator running? — Then you'd better go catch it!'), the 'Prince Albert' gag, and name-based double-entendre calls exemplified by Bart Simpson's calls to Moe's Tavern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These formats are historically common and recognizable; they tend to be low-risk comedic devices but have cultural recognizability rather than being inherently harmless in all contexts. Repeating familiar tropes may reduce originality but increase immediate audience recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community dissemination and archival practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Recorded prank calls became staples of cassette tape trading (late 1970s) and later online communities; internet radio rotations, user-generated content, and forums allow widespread sharing and community feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how distribution and archiving affect both popularity and consequences: broad sharing can amplify harm and legal exposure; communities (e.g., soundboard followers, Pranknet) may normalize risky behavior and coordinate harmful pranks.
